data:
A cell is Go with statements allowed at the top level, as in a REPL:
import "strings" func words(s string) []string { return strings.Fields(s) } w := words("to be or not to be") len(w) // the final expression is shown $ notebook run words.md ── cell 0 (line 4, ran in 86µs) 6
data.declarations-and-statements#Declarations: Top-level func, type and import are declarations of the notebook. Everything else is a statement of the cell, run in order. The names a cell defines at its top level — by :=, var, const, func or type — are notebook variables: every cell, and every function, can read them.
data.errors-point-at-the-notebook#Errors poin:
The generated program carries //line directives, so compiler errors and panic stacks name the notebook’s own lines, not the generated file’s.
A cell that fails stops the cells that read it, and they say why:
```go var xs []int first := xs[0] ``` ```go first + 1 ``` $ notebook run panic.md ── cell 0 (line 4, ran in 104µs) error: panic: runtime error: index out of range [0] with length 0 … main._nbcell0(…) …/panic.md:5 +0x3c … ── cell 1 (line 9, kept) error: not run: cell 0 failed notebook: 2 cell(s) failed (The stack is shortened here; the frame of the cell names panic.md:5, the line of xs[0].)
data.no-assignment-to-another-cells-variable#:
A cell may not assign to a variable another cell defines: the dependency graph would not see the change.
```go x := 1 ``` ```go x = 2 ``` $ notebook run rules.md … error: 8:1: cell 1: cannot assign to x, which cell 0 defines; define a new name instead notebook: 1 cell(s) failed Mutation through a method or a slice element cannot be seen statically and is not refused (marimo makes the same choice).
data.one-definition-per-name#One definition p: Each notebook variable is defined by exactly one cell. Go already forbids two package-level declarations of a name, which gives this rule for free.
data.private-names-stay-in-their-cell#Private: A name starting with _, and err — which nearly every cell declares and none means to share — are local to their cell. Two cells may each have their own err.
data.the-final-expression-is-shown#The final:
A cell’s final expression statement is its display value. A call with several results (fmt.Println’s n, err) is run for its effect and not shown.
A value with a Display() map[string][]byte method (the runtime.Displayer interface) shows itself: the map goes from a MIME type — text/plain, text/html, image/svg+xml, image/png, … — to the bytes of that representation. Values without one show their %v.
What a cell prints, through os.Stdout, the println builtin or C code, is captured and shown with it. (On systems without dup2 — Windows, js, wasip1 — os.Stdout and os.Stderr are swapped instead, and println is not captured.)
data.the-three-rules#The three rules: They make the order of execution a function of the code, as in marimo, rather than of the order cells were run in.
data.variables-that-cannot-be-shared#Variable: A notebook variable becomes a package-level variable of the generated program, which needs its type to be written there. A variable whose type cannot be written outside its package (an unexported type) cannot be shared: the error says so and suggests a private name (_x).

data: go install github.com/go-notebook/notebook/cmd/notebook@latest usage: notebook run|html|watch|serve [flags] notebook.md run run the notebook and print each cell's results html run it and write the results as a page next to it (or -o) watch run it again every time the file changes, keeping the page current serve run it again every time the file changes, showing it live in a browser (-addr) Edit the .md in any editor. Every verb goes through the same kernel, so each one runs only the cells whose code or inputs changed since the last run of that notebook, whichever verb ran it (see The kernel).
data.flags#Flags: Flag Default Verbs Meaning -o .html html, watch the HTML file to write -addr 127.0.0.1:8888 serve where serve listens -interval 300ms watch, serve how often the file is looked at -work under the user cache directory all the work directory -runtime-src all use the go-notebook source tree at this path instead of a released runtime Flags go between the verb and the notebook: notebook html -o out.html nb.md.
data.html#html: notebook html analysis.md # writes analysis.html notebook html -o report.html analysis.md Runs the notebook and writes a standalone HTML page: the prose rendered as Markdown, each code cell with what it printed, showed or failed with. The page has no scripts and no external resources, and raw HTML in the prose is left out (goldmark’s safe default), so a page made from someone else’s notebook runs nothing of theirs but what its cells chose to display.
data.run#run:
notebook run analysis.md Runs the notebook and prints each code cell: its index, its line in the file, and either how long it ran or kept when its result was kept from before; then what it printed, what it showed and its error, indented.
$ notebook run spectrum.md ── cell 0 (line 4, kept) ── cell 1 (line 12, kept) ── cell 2 (line 19, ran in 42µs) 9.54929284535666e-07 The exit status is non-zero when a cell failed (notebook: 1 cell(s) failed), so notebook run can gate a CI job.
data.serve#serve:
notebook serve analysis.md notebook serve -addr 127.0.0.1:9000 analysis.md The same loop as watch, but the page is served at -addr (default 127.0.0.1:8888) instead of written to a file:
$ notebook serve spectrum.md serving spectrum.md at http://127.0.0.1:8888/ 21:28:21 0 of 3 cells ran, build 252ms: ok The page reloads itself through a server-sent event when the results change, and keeps its scroll position. A notebook that cannot run at all (for example, an import that cannot be fetched) is shown as an error page instead of a stale one. The served page is the html page plus the small script that reloads it.
data.the-runtime-the-notebook-links#The runti: The compiled notebook links package runtime of go-notebook. A notebook installed from a release tag makes the notebook’s work module require that same release. A notebook built from a source checkout uses that checkout instead (through a replace directive), since its pseudo-version names no published runtime with the same code; -runtime-src points at a checkout explicitly.
data.the-work-directory#The work directory: By default each notebook has its own work directory under the user’s cache directory (go-notebook/
data.watch#watch:
notebook watch analysis.md Runs the notebook every time the file changes, and keeps analysis.html (or -o) current. Each run prints one line:
21:28:21 0 of 3 cells ran, build 252ms: ok It looks at the file’s modification time every -interval (300 ms by default), and runs until interrupted.

data: Mirrored from docs/design.md in go-notebook/notebook at main 1cc66fc. Everything from the first section on is that file, verbatim.
data.a-cell-is-go-with-top-level-statements#A:
import "math" func sq(x float64) float64 { return x * x } y := sq(math.Pi) y Top-level func, type and import are declarations of the notebook. The rest is the cell’s statements, run in order. The names a cell defines at the top level (:=, var, const, func, type) are notebook variables, readable from every cell. A final expression is the cell’s display value; a call with several results (fmt.Println’s n, err) is run for its effect and not shown.
Three rules make the order a function of the code, as in marimo:
One definition per name. Go already forbids two package-level declarations of a name, which gives this rule for free. No assignment to another cell’s variable. The dependency graph would not see the change. Mutation through a method or an element cannot be seen statically and is not refused (marimo makes the same choice). Private names stay in their cell: a name starting with _, and err, which nearly every cell declares and none means to share.
data.a-notebook-is-a-markdown-file#A notebook:
Its ```go blocks are the cells; everything else is prose, kept byte for byte (format.Parse(src).String() == src for every input; it is fuzzed). GitHub and every Markdown viewer show a notebook as a document, and a diff of a notebook is a diff of text. No output is ever written into it.
A valid Go file was considered first and rejected. Go allows no statements at the top level, and x := load(path) or fmt.Println(x) at the top level of a cell is most of what a notebook is. Wrapping every cell in a function costs the user more than editor support on the raw file gains. The kernel produces the valid Go program instead; see below.
data.dependencies-come-from-syntax-types-come:
analysis finds each cell’s definitions and free identifiers from the parse alone, so it works on code that does not compile yet. Those give the graph, its order and its errors (cycles, double definitions, foreign assignments).
gen writes the program. Each cell becomes a function. Its variables become package-level variables, which needs their types: gen type-checks the cells one by one in dependency order to learn them. The cells’ text is kept as it is and edited in place: := becomes = , var x T becomes x = *new(T) so that running the cell again resets it, constants move to package level, and the display value is wrapped in _k.Show(...). /*line nb.md:L:C*/ directives point every line back into the notebook, so compiler errors and panic stacks name the notebook’s own lines.
A variable whose type cannot be written outside its package (an unexported type) cannot be shared. The error says so and suggests a private name.
data.display#Display: runtime.Displayer is a MIME bundle: Display() map[string][]byte with text/plain, text/html, image/svg+xml, image/png… Values without one show their %v.
data.native-code-kept-values#Native code, kep:
The kernel compiles the program into a worker process. Go’s build cache makes rebuilding after a one-cell edit cost about a tenth of a second here. The kernel then does the least work that brings the results up to date:
A cell’s key is a hash of its source, the import paths of the packages it refers to, the Go toolchain’s version, the work module’s go.sum when the cell uses a package outside the standard library, and the keys of the cells it reads. Its position is not part of it, so moving cells runs nothing; neither does an import another cell adds. Upgrading Go, or a dependency, runs again what it could change. An unchanged key keeps its result. After a rebuild, the variables the cell made are handed to the new worker, not computed again. Values are encoded with their own MarshalBinary when they have one, and with gob when every field they can hold is exported (gob would silently drop the others). Anything else is volatile: its cell runs again, but only when a cell that reads it has to run. Results and values are kept on disk in the work directory, so a new kernel, or the next notebook run, starts where the last one stopped. A failing cell stops its readers, which report why. A worker that dies (os.Exit, a crash outside the recovered call) is restarted on the next run. This assumes a cell computes the same values from the same inputs. A cell that reads the clock or an unseeded generator should be run explicitly (Kernel.RunCell).
data.not-yet#Not yet: A Jupyter wire-protocol front end (JupyterLab, VS Code), and a go-widgets native and wasm UI. Running independent branches of the graph concurrently. Real LaTeX in prose through go-tex; for now $...$ stays as text. MarshalBinary on go-ndarray arrays, so that arrays are kept rather than volatile.
data.output-capture#Output capture: What a cell prints, through os.Stdout, the println builtin or C code, is captured by pointing file descriptors 1 and 2 at a pipe for the duration of the cell. The protocol replies travel on a duplicate of the original standard output, so a cell can never forge one. Systems without dup2 (Windows, js, wasip1) swap os.Stdout and os.Stderr instead, and do not capture println.
data.what-exists-and-what-each-gets-wrong#Wha: execution state between cells order speed Jupyter (Python) interpreter, one process values, hidden and mutable whatever order the cells were clicked in interpreted; numpy in C gophernotes gomacro interpreter values clicked order interpreted Go; generics partial GoNB compiles the cell plus the declarations it memorised, then runs it declarations only — values are computed again on every run (it ships a cache package as the workaround) clicked order native marimo (Python) interpreter values reactive graph from static analysis; one definition per name interpreted None has native speed, kept values and a reproducible order together. go-notebook is built to have all three.

data: Each run takes the notebook’s current code cells and does the least work that brings every result up to date. Four steps get there: the analysis of the cells, the generated program, the cell keys, and the value store.
data.a-cells-key#A cell’s key:
A cell’s key is a hash of:
its source; the import paths of the packages it refers to; the Go toolchain’s version; the work module’s go.sum, when the cell uses a package outside the standard library (any module could be behind such a package, transitively, so the whole go.sum is the honest summary); the keys of the cells it reads. Its position is not part of the key, so moving cells runs nothing; neither does an import another cell adds. Upgrading Go, or a dependency, runs again what it could change, and only that: a cell using only the standard library is not run again by a go.sum change. Because a key includes the keys of its inputs, a change propagates to exactly the cells downstream of it.
data.kept-values#Kept values:
To hand a value over, or to keep it on disk, the kernel encodes it:
with its own MarshalBinary when it has one; with gob when every field it can hold is exported (gob would silently drop the others). Anything else — a func, a channel, unexported state — is volatile: its cell runs again, but only when a cell that reads it has to run.
data.on-disk#On disk: Results and values are kept in the work directory, so a new kernel, or the next notebook run, starts where the last one stopped. The notebook command gives each notebook its own work directory under the user’s cache directory.
data.the-assumption#The assumption: All of this assumes a cell computes the same values from the same inputs. A cell that reads the clock or an unseeded random generator does not; such a cell should be run explicitly — Kernel.RunCell runs a cell again even if nothing changed, together with every cell that reads it.
data.the-dependency-graph#The dependency grap:
Package analysis finds each cell’s definitions and free identifiers from the parse alone. It needs no type information, so it works on code that does not compile yet.
A cell depends on the cells that define the names it reads. That gives the graph, the order of execution, and the static errors: cycles, double definitions and assignments to another cell’s variable (see Cells). The order is therefore a function of the code, never of the order cells were run in or appear in.
data.the-generated-program#The generated prog:
Package gen writes the Go program the kernel compiles:
each cell becomes a function; its variables become package-level variables, so every cell can read them and their values outlive the call. That needs their types, so gen type-checks the cells one by one, in dependency order, with go/types; the cells’ text is kept as it is and edited in place: := becomes = , var x T becomes x = *new(T) (so running the cell again resets it), constants move to package level, and the display value is wrapped in a call that shows it; //line nb.md:L:C directives point every line back into the notebook. The kernel compiles this program into a worker process and drives it through package runtime: one JSON request per line on the worker’s standard input (run, get, set, exit) and one reply per line on its standard output. What a cell prints goes to a pipe of its own, so it can never be mistaken for a reply.
Go’s build cache makes rebuilding after a one-cell edit cost about a tenth of a second.
data.using-the-kernel-from-go#Using the kerne: k, err := kernel.New(kernel.Options{Dir: work, Name: "analysis.md"}) if err != nil { … } defer k.Close() rep, err := k.Run(cells) // cells: []gen.Code{{Source: …, Line: …}, …} for _, r := range rep.Results { // r.Ran, r.Took, r.Output, r.Display, r.Error } Report.Built says whether the worker was rebuilt, Report.Build how long generating and building took, and Report.Diags holds the static errors.
data.what-runs#What runs:
A cell whose key… … did not change keeps its result and is not run changed runs, and so does every cell whose key changes because of it did not change, but made a volatile value that a running cell reads runs again, to make that value (see below) reads a cell that failed is not run, and reports not run: cell N failed When the program changes, the worker is rebuilt and restarted. The variables made by unchanged cells are handed to the new worker instead of being computed again.
A worker that dies (os.Exit, a crash outside the recovered call) is restarted on the next run.

data:
A notebook is a Markdown file. Its fenced code blocks whose info string’s first word is go are code cells; everything between them is prose, kept byte for byte.
# Spectrum Some prose, with a list, a table, a link: any Markdown. ```go x := 40 + 2 ``` ```python # A block in another language is prose, not a cell. ```
data.fences#Fences: Fences follow CommonMark: three or more backticks or tildes, indented by at most three spaces, closed by a fence of the same character at least as long. A code block in another language is prose.
data.nothing-is-written-back#Nothing is writt:
No output is ever stored in the file. Results live in the kernel’s value store (see The kernel) and in exports such as the HTML page written by notebook html.
Because of that:
GitHub, and every Markdown viewer, shows a notebook as a document; a diff of a notebook is a diff of text, with no execution counts or outputs; reading and writing a notebook round-trips exactly: format.Parse(src).String() == src for every input, and that property is fuzzed.
data.the-packages#The packages: The Markdown is read and written by package format. Its Parse returns a Notebook whose Cells are either code or prose, each with its line in the file.
data.why-not-a-valid-go-file#Why not a valid: A .go file was considered first and rejected. Go allows no statements at the top level, and x := load(path) or fmt.Println(x) at the top level of a cell is most of what a notebook is. Wrapping every cell in a function costs the user more than editor support on the raw file gains. The kernel produces the valid Go program instead: see The kernel.
